sources.title: Mediators Meet with Kagame and M23 Rebels on DR Congo Peace Process
sources.excerpt: African Union Delegation Holds Talks in Rwanda and Goma as Conflict Escalates in Eastern DRC. On Wednesday, a delegation of African Union (AU) mediators met with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and with representatives of the Congolese rebel group March 23 Movement (M23) to address the peace process in eastern…
sources.text: Mediators Meet with Kagame and M23 Rebels on DR Congo Peace Process. On Wednesday, a delegation of African Union (AU) mediators met with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and with representatives of the Congolese rebel group March 23 Movement (M23) to address the peace process in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). “This afternoon at Urugwiro Village, President Kagame met with a delegation of members of the AU panel of mediators for the peace process in eastern DRC,” the Rwandan Presidency said. Among the AU mediators are former Ethiopian President Sahle-Work Zewde, former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta and former Botswanan President Mokgweetsi Masisi. During the meeting, both parties spoke about the next steps to achieve a “lasting and stable” peace in eastern Congo, as well as the main causes of the conflict. The same mediation team met Monday with M23 in the Congolese city of Goma, capital of North Kivu province and under rebel control, and in which the United Nations Mission in the DRC (Monusco), the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus (EJVM) also participated. “These meetings provided the opportunity to listen to different perspectives on the peace process, the humanitarian and security situation, and the measures needed to strengthen trust,” the AU said. The mediators called for “strict respect” of cease-fire commitments, as well as cooperation with the mechanisms for verifying it. They also underscored the “urgent need” to protect the civilian population, prevent sexual and gender-based violence, and guarantee both accountability for violations committed and “safe and unhindered” humanitarian access. The conflict worsened at the end of January 2025, when M23 took control of Goma and, weeks later, of Bukavu, capital of South Kivu province (east), after clashes with the Congolese Army. Since Congolese President Felix Tshisekedi and Rwandan President Paul Kagame signed a peace agreement on Dec. 4, 2025, in Washington in the presence of U.S. President Donald Trump, who ratified the June 2025 pact, both parties have accused each other of violating it. That agreement adds to the mediation efforts sponsored by Qatar between the Congolese Government and M23, which on Nov. 15, 2025, signed a framework agreement in Doha. Eastern DRC, rich in minerals essential to the technology industry, has experienced since the 1990s a conflict fueled by rebel groups and the Army, despite the deployment of the Monusco mission.

sources.title: Six Ebola Cases Reported in M23-Held Congo
sources.excerpt: Six new Ebola cases, including four people who died before testing, were reported in AFC/M23-controlled eastern Congo, with all linked to a transmission chain originating in government-held Butembo.
sources.text: Six Ebola Cases Reported in M23-Held Congo. Six new Ebola cases have been reported in AFC/M23-controlled areas of eastern Democratic Republic of Congo: four in Alimbongo and two in Kayna. Health officials say the infections belong to one transmission chain linked to a case from government-held Butembo; four people died before post-mortem tests confirmed Ebola, while two patients are receiving care. Teams are stepping up surveillance and contact tracing as the outbreak continues to spread. Nationwide, the outbreak has caused 4,018 deaths among 8,300 confirmed cases, and health agencies warn that insecurity and public mistrust are hampering efforts to contain it. Kenya confirmed its first Ebola death: Aden Duale said a Bundibugyo case patient regrettably passed on last night at around 1130 after reaching Nairobi on Oct. 3.

sources.title: M23’s Grip on Congo’s Mines is Turning Minerals into a War Economy
sources.excerpt: Rwanda-backed M23 fighters have killed, tortured and forcibly recruited artisanal miners in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and helped traffic gold and coltan into Rwanda, Amnesty International ...
sources.text: M23’s Grip on Congo’s Mines is Turning Minerals into a War Economy. Rwanda-backed M23 fighters have killed, tortured and forcibly recruited artisanal miners in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and helped traffic gold and coltan into Rwanda, Amnesty International says, allegations that could amount to war crimes and expose companies buying the minerals to legal and reputational risks. The rights group said its investigation, published on Sept. 21, documented abuses at a coltan mine near Rubaya in North Kivu province and a gold mine at Lomera in South Kivu, including summary killings, forced labour, arbitrary detention and torture. Amnesty interviewed 26 people, including miners, mine-shaft owners, mining experts and relatives of victims, and analysed photographs and videos from the mining areas. “Rwanda-backed M23 is committing horrific human rights abuses, which may amount to war crimes, against artisanal miners in eastern DRC. These are meant to punish and instill fear among miners and others living and working near the mines, as minerals are trafficked across the border into Rwanda, which has continued to profit from the exploitation of DRC’s mineral wealth,” said Agnes Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General. Amnesty said it documented the killing of 18 artisanal miners at Rubaya and Lomera, with witnesses and relatives saying 10 were beaten to death, two were shot and six people who had been abducted were later found dead. Sixteen miners or civilians living near the sites also described being tortured or otherwise mistreated, while more than 20 miners at Rubaya were allegedly held in underground detention cells and beaten three times a day. The allegations add to longstanding international scrutiny of the mineral trade between eastern Congo and Rwanda, where armed groups, traders and regional authorities have been accused of exploiting supply chains that connect conflict zones to global markets for electronics and other products. The Democratic Republic of Congo was the world’s largest producer of tantalum in 2024, accounting for an estimated 51% of global output, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. Tantalum, derived in part from coltan ore, is used in electronic components because of its resistance to heat and corrosion. The USGS estimated Congo’s tantalum mine production at 1,300 metric tons in 2025, compared with 400 tons for Rwanda. Rwanda was nevertheless the world’s third-largest tantalum producer in 2024, accounting for about 15% of global production, according to the USGS. Its mineral exports were worth $3.2 billion in 2024, with gold accounting for 47% of the total and niobium and tantalum for 3.1%. The discrepancy between Rwanda’s relatively small domestic tantalum production and its role as a regional trading and processing hub has been a focus of international scrutiny. The U.S. State Department said in a 2024 statement that credible reporting indicated Rwanda remained a destination and processing hub for illegally mined critical minerals and gold originating in eastern Congo, while noting that existing traceability schemes faced questions over their effectiveness. A 2025 report by a United Nations Security Council sanctions-monitoring group found that M23 had exploited coltan, cassiterite and other minerals at numerous sites around Rubaya and controlled trading centres and mineral transport routes. The report said M23 had established a monopoly over coltan exports from Rubaya to Rwanda and that minerals from the area were mixed with Rwandan production. The United Nations report described the Rubaya trade as a significant contamination of mineral supply chains in the Great Lakes region, while saying the group’s control of the area allowed it to benefit from taxes and mineral trading. Another UN document said the seizure of Rubaya in April 2024 appeared to have been driven in part by a strategic effort to control the mineral evacuation route and make Rwanda the principal transit market for coltan from the area. Amnesty said its researchers found evidence that gold was being moved from Lomera to Rwanda through established smuggling routes. According to interviews and evidence reviewed by its Evidence Lab, sacks containing gold-bearing soil were loaded onto boats at the Port of Lomera and transported across Lake Kivu to a collection site in Kamembe, in Rwanda’s Western province. One Congolese miner who worked at Lomera said: “I was there at night. I hid and saw that [M23] sent three groups … to different mineshafts. They took the mineralized sand [soil containing gold] and took it near the lake…When they arrived, they put it in small boats and sent it to Rwanda.” Another miner said: “We saw [boats being loaded]. Loaded with robotas [sacks of soil containing gold]. They did this very early in the morning. Each morning, they came with traders from Rwanda. And the same boats came at night.” Amnesty said it believed the seizure and trafficking of gold and coltan by M23 could constitute the war crime of pillage. It also said the involvement of Rwandans in the mines and the movement of minerals into Rwanda could expose the Rwandan state and individuals to international legal responsibility, depending on evidence of direction or control. “This investigation should serve as a wake-up call to Rwanda that Rwandans may bear international criminal responsibility for facilitating the trafficking of pillaged minerals to Rwanda,” said Callamard. “Rwanda may also bear state responsibility for the horrific abuses against miners if Rwandans in the mines are acting under the direction or control of Rwanda, even if they are not employees of the government.” Amnesty said miners interviewed at Rubaya reported that Rwandans worked both as civilian miners and mine-shaft managers and, in some cases, participated alongside M23 fighters. It also said some security guards at Rubaya and Lomera identified themselves as Rwandan or spoke Kinyarwanda and were alleged to have collaborated with M23 in beating and mistreating miners. sources.text: M23 rebellion (2012–2013). The First M23 rebellion was an armed conflict in North Kivu, Democratic Republic of the Congo, that occurred between the March 23 Movement (M23) rebel group and Congolese government forces between 4 April 2012 and 7 November 2013. It ended when a peace agreement was made among eleven African nations, and the M23 troops surrendered in Uganda. The rebellion was part of continued fighting in the region after the formal end of the Second Congo War in 2003. The conflict reignited in late 2021 after M23 rebel leader Sultani Makenga and 100 rebel fighters attacked the border town of Bunagana but failed. A few months later, M23 rebels officially restarted offensive operations, rapidly expanding their control over vast regions of North Kivu.
